{{Short description|Inequality in probability theorem}}
In [[probability theory]], '''Cantelli's inequality''' (also called the '''Chebyshev-Cantelli inequality''' and the '''one-sided Chebyshev inequality''') is an improved version of [[Chebyshev's inequality]] for one-sided tail bounds.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Boucheron|first=Stéphane|title=Concentration inequalities : a nonasymptotic theory of independence|date=2013|publisher=Oxford University Press|others=Gábor Lugosi, Pascal Massart|isbn=978-0-19-953525-5|location=Oxford|oclc=829910957}}</ref><ref>[http://www.cse.buffalo.edu/~hungngo/classes/2011/Spring-694/lectures/l4.pdf "Tail and Concentration Inequalities" by Hung Q. Ngo]</ref><ref>[http://www.econ.upf.edu/~lugosi/anu.pdf "Concentration-of-measure inequalities" by Gábor Lugosi]</ref> The inequality states that, for <math>\lambda > 0,</math>

: <math>
\Pr(X-\mathbb{E}[X]\ge\lambda)
\le \frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + \lambda^2},
</math>

where

:<math>X</math> is a real-valued [[random variable]],
:<math>\Pr</math> is the [[probability measure]],
:<math>\mathbb{E}[X]</math> is the [[expected value]] of <math>X</math>,
:<math>\sigma^2</math> is the [[variance]] of <math>X</math>.

Applying the Cantelli inequality to <math>-X</math> gives a bound on the lower tail,

: <math>
\Pr(X-\mathbb{E}[X]\le -\lambda)
\le \frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + \lambda^2}.
</math>

While the inequality is often attributed to [[Francesco Paolo Cantelli]] who published it in 1928,<ref>Cantelli, F. P. (1928), "Sui confini della probabilita," Atti del Congresso Internazional del Matematici, Bologna, 6, 47-5</ref> it originates in Chebyshev's work of 1874.<ref>[https://www.jstor.org/stable/3087296 Ghosh, B.K., 2002. Probability inequalities related to Markov's theorem. ''The American Statistician'', 56(3), pp.186-190]</ref> When bounding the event random variable deviates from its [[expected value|mean]] in only one direction (positive or negative), Cantelli's inequality gives an improvement over Chebyshev's inequality. The Chebyshev inequality has [[Chebyshev's inequality#Higher moments|"higher moments versions"]] and [[Chebyshev's inequality#Vector version|"vector versions"]], and so does the Cantelli inequality.

== Comparison to Chebyshev's inequality ==

For one-sided tail bounds, Cantelli's inequality is better, since Chebyshev's inequality can only get

: <math>
\Pr(X - \mathbb{E}[X] \geq \lambda) \leq \Pr(|X-\mathbb{E}[X]|\ge\lambda)
\le \frac{\sigma^2}{\lambda^2}.
</math>

On the other hand, for two-sided tail bounds, Cantelli's inequality gives

: <math>
\Pr(|X-\mathbb{E}[X]|\ge\lambda)
= \Pr(X-\mathbb{E}[X]\ge\lambda) + \Pr(X-\mathbb{E}[X]\le-\lambda)
\le \frac{2\sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + \lambda^2},
</math>

which is always worse than Chebyshev's inequality (when <math>\lambda \geq \sigma</math>; otherwise, both inequalities bound a probability by a value greater than one, and so are trivial).

==Generalizations==

Various stronger inequalities can be shown.
He, Zhang, and Zhang showed<ref name=He2010>{{cite journal | last1 = He | first1 = S. | last2 = Zhang | first2 = J. | last3 = Zhang | first3 = S. | s2cid = 11298475 | year = 2010 | title = Bounding probability of small deviation: A fourth moment approach | journal = Mathematics of Operations Research | volume = 35 | issue = 1| pages = 208–232 | doi = 10.1287/moor.1090.0438 }}</ref> (Corollary 2.3)  when
<math>\mathbb{E}[X]=0,\,\mathbb{E}[X^2]=1</math> and <math>\lambda\ge0</math>:

: <math>
\Pr(X\ge\lambda) \le 1- (2\sqrt{3}-3)\frac{(1+\lambda^2)^2}{\mathbb{E}[X^4]+6\lambda^2+\lambda^4}.
</math>

In the case <math>\lambda=0</math> this matches a bound in Berger's "The Fourth Moment Method",<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Berger |first=Bonnie |date=August 1997 |title=The Fourth Moment Method |url=http://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/S0097539792240005 |journal=SIAM Journal on Computing |language=en |volume=26 |issue=4 |pages=1188–1207 |doi=10.1137/S0097539792240005 |s2cid=14313557 |issn=0097-5397|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
: <math>
\Pr(X\ge 0) \ge \frac{2\sqrt{3}-3}{\mathbb{E}[X^4]}.
</math>
This improves over Cantelli's inequality in that we can get a non-zero lower bound, even when <math>\mathbb{E}[X]=0</math>.
